summary.en: Venezuelan authorities have detained former world champion boxer Linares on US immigration charges while appointing a gay man as foreign minister, indicating internal political shifts. The government has accused Uruguay's president of interference over calls for free elections and granted a US-backed firm 100-year control of 17 oil fields, expanding foreign involvement in the oil sector. Cuba has activated wartime structures in response to US President Trump's statements about Cuba, and a special forces soldier who bet $400,000 on Maduro's capture pleaded not guilty, showing personal stakes in the conflict. 2 battle-related deaths were recorded in 2007, according to UCDP.
summary.nb: Venezuelanske myndigheter har arrestert den tidligere verdensmesteren i boksing, Linares, på amerikanske immigrasjonsanklager mens de utnevnte en homofil mann til utenriksminister, noe som indikerer interne politiske skift. Regjeringen har anklaget Uruguays president for innblanding over oppfordringer til frie valg og har gitt et amerikansk-støttet firma 100‑årig kontroll over 17 oljefelt, noe som utvider utenlandsk involvering i oljesektoren. Cuba har aktivert krigstidstrukturer som svar på USAs president Trumps uttalelser om Cuba, og en spesialstyrkesoldat som satset 400 000 $ på at Maduro skulle bli tatt, erklærte seg ikke skyldig, noe som viser personlige interesser i konflikten. To dødsfall knyttet til kamper ble registrert i 2007, ifølge UCDP.

background.title: Crisis in Venezuela
background.extract: An ongoing socioeconomic and political crisis began in Venezuela during the presidencies of Hugo Chávez, Nicolás Maduro as well as Delcy Rodríguez. It has been marked by hyperinflation, starvation, disease, crime, and mortality rates, resulting in massive emigration. Food shortages and hyperinflation have ended, but inflation remains high. It is the worst economic crisis in Venezuela's history and considered by some sources as more severe than the Great Depression in the United States, the 1985–1994 Brazilian economic crisis, or the 2008–2009 hyperinflation in Zimbabwe. In 2019, the Institute of International Finance called it the single largest economic collapse outside of war in 45 years. Writers have compared aspects, such as unemployment and GDP contraction, to Bosnia and Herzegovina after the 1992–95 Bosnian War, and those in Russia, Cuba and Albania following the Revolutions of 1989.
